preamble.summary: Chapter 19 warns against the dangers of wine and loose living, then devotes extensive attention to the ethics of gossip, rumor, and tale-bearing. The chapter concludes with a reflection on the difference between true wisdom rooted in the fear of the Lord and mere cleverness used for wicked ends.
preamble.remarkable: Ben Sira's treatment of gossip is among the most psychologically acute in ancient literature. He does not simply condemn tale-bearing but walks through the social dynamics: the urge to repeat what one has heard, the distortion that inevitably occurs, and the obligation to confront a friend directly rather than spreading rumors. The closing distinction between wisdom and cunning (vv. 20-27) is a penetrating moral insight -- intelligence without moral orientation is worse than ignorance.
preamble.friction: The opening warning that 'a worker given to drunkenness will not grow rich' (v. 1) strikes a utilitarian note that sits uneasily beside the chapter's later moral idealism. The idea that one can discern a person's character from physical appearance (v. 26) reflects ancient physiognomic assumptions that modern readers will find problematic.
preamble.connections: Proverbs 20:1 (wine is a mocker); Leviticus 19:17 (rebuke your neighbor frankly); James 1:19 (slow to speak); Proverbs 11:13 (a gossip betrays a confidence).

verses.text_latin: Operarius ebriosus non locupletabitur et qui spernit modica paulatim decidet.
verses.rendering: A worker given to drunkenness will not grow rich, and whoever despises small things will fall little by little.
translator_notes: Two proverbs joined by the theme of incremental self-destruction through lack of discipline.

key_terms.note: Not a single episode but a habitual condition -- the adjective marks chronic intemperance.

verses.text_latin: Vinum et mulieres apostatare faciunt sapientes et arguent sensatos.
verses.rendering: Wine and women make wise men fall away, and they will bring the sensible into disgrace.
translator_notes: A conventional ancient Near Eastern pairing of intoxication and sexual temptation as twin threats to wisdom.

key_terms.note: The Latin apostatare carries the strong sense of apostasy -- abandonment of one's commitment to wisdom, not merely a lapse in judgment.

verses.text_latin: Et qui se iungit fornicariis erit nequam putredo et vermes hereditabunt illum et extolletur in exemplum maius et tolletur de numero anima eius.
verses.rendering: And whoever consorts with prostitutes will become depraved; decay and worms will inherit him, and he will be held up as a greater warning, and his soul will be removed from the number of the living.

verses.text_latin: Qui credit cito levis est corde et minorabitur et qui delinquit in animam suam insuper habebitur.
verses.rendering: Whoever trusts too quickly is light of heart and will be diminished; and whoever sins against his own soul will be held in contempt.

key_terms.note: Not cheerful but lacking gravity -- the 'light heart' is gullible and unstable, the opposite of the wise person's measured deliberation.

verses.text_latin: Qui gaudet iniquitate denotabitur et qui odit correptionem minuetur vita et qui odit loquacitatem extinguit malitiam.
verses.rendering: Whoever delights in wickedness will be condemned, and whoever hates correction will have his life shortened; but whoever hates gossip quenches evil.
translator_notes: The triad moves from vice to correction-refusal to the pivotal theme of the chapter: the destructive power of careless speech.

key_terms.note: Latin loquacitas can mean mere talkativeness, but in this moral context it implies harmful, uncontrolled speech -- gossip.

verses.text_latin: Qui peccat in animam suam paenitebit et qui iucundatur in malitia denotabitur.
verses.rendering: Whoever sins against his own soul will repent of it, and whoever takes pleasure in malice will be condemned.

verses.text_latin: Ne iteres verbum nequam et durum et non minoraberis.
verses.rendering: Do not repeat a wicked and harsh word, and you will not be diminished.
translator_notes: The simplest form of the chapter's central ethic: stop the chain of harmful speech at yourself.

verses.text_latin: Amico et inimico noli enarrare sensum tuum et si est tibi delictum noli denudare.
verses.rendering: To neither friend nor enemy reveal your private thoughts, and if you have a fault, do not expose it.

verses.text_latin: Audiet enim te et custodiet te et quasi defendens peccatum odiet te et sic aderit tibi semper.
verses.rendering: For he will listen to you and watch you, and while pretending to defend your sin, he will hate you -- and so he will be at your side always.
translator_notes: A keen observation of social duplicity: the false friend who listens sympathetically while storing ammunition.

verses.text_latin: Audisti verbum adversus proximum tuum commoriatur in te fidens quoniam non te disrumpet.
verses.rendering: Have you heard a word against your neighbor? Let it die within you, trusting that it will not burst you apart.
translator_notes: The image is almost physical -- the rumor presses to escape, but the disciplined person contains it and lets it expire.

key_terms.note: A vivid metaphor: the gossip should literally 'die with you' -- be buried rather than passed along.

verses.text_latin: A facie verbi parturit fatuus tamquam gemitus partus infantis.
verses.rendering: At the face of a word, a fool goes into labor, like the groaning of a woman giving birth.
translator_notes: The fool cannot contain a secret; it causes him physical agony until he delivers it forth -- a comic but cutting image.

verses.text_latin: Sagitta infixa femori carnis sic verbum in corde stulti.
verses.rendering: Like an arrow stuck in the flesh of the thigh, so is a word in the heart of a fool.
translator_notes: The secret lodged in a fool is an irritant that demands removal -- he must speak it out or suffer.

verses.text_latin: Corripe amicum ne forte non intellexerit et dicat non feci aut si fecit ne iterum adiciat facere.
verses.rendering: Confront your friend, lest perhaps he did not understand, so that he may say, 'I did not do it'; or if he did, so that he may not do it again.
translator_notes: Direct confrontation is presented as the ethical alternative to gossip -- a principle rooted in Leviticus 19:17.

verses.text_latin: Corripe proximum antequam comminetur et da locum timori Altissimi.
verses.rendering: Confront your neighbor before he threatens you, and give place to the fear of the Most High.

key_terms.note: The fear of God provides the moral framework for honest confrontation -- it is not personal aggression but obedience to a higher standard.

verses.text_latin: Quia non est omnis in omni sapientia et non est omnis homo in omni sensu.
verses.rendering: For not everyone has wisdom in every matter, and not every person has understanding in all things.
translator_notes: A charitable assumption: honest ignorance is possible, so confrontation should be exploratory rather than accusatory.

verses.text_latin: Omnis sapientia timor Dei et in omni sapientia dispositio legis.
verses.rendering: All wisdom is the fear of God, and in all wisdom there is the fulfillment of the law.
translator_notes: This verse functions as the theological spine of the chapter: genuine wisdom is inseparable from reverence for God and obedience to Torah.

key_terms.note: Latin dispositio implies orderly arrangement or implementation -- wisdom is Torah put into practice, not merely known.

verses.text_latin: Et non est sapientia nequitiae disciplina et non est cogitatus peccatorum prudentia.
verses.rendering: The discipline of wickedness is not wisdom, and the thinking of sinners is not prudence.
translator_notes: A critical distinction: cleverness in evil is not true wisdom. Moral orientation is an essential property of wisdom, not an optional addition.

verses.text_latin: Est nequitia et in ipsa execratio et est insipiens qui minuitur sapientia.
verses.rendering: There is a cleverness that is abomination, and there is a fool who merely lacks wisdom.

key_terms.note: Nequitia here denotes not mere wickedness but cunning -- intelligence deployed for evil, which is worse than simple foolishness.

verses.text_latin: Melior est qui minuitur sapientia et deficit sensu in timore quam qui abundat sensu et transgreditur legem.
verses.rendering: Better is one who lacks wisdom and is deficient in understanding but fears God, than one who abounds in understanding yet transgresses the law.
translator_notes: The hierarchy is clear: moral fear of God outranks intellectual ability. This is a direct challenge to Greek philosophical assumptions about the primacy of knowledge.

verses.text_latin: Est sollertia certa et ipsa iniqua et est qui pervertit gratiam ut ostendat iudicium et est iustus qui se nimium submittit.
verses.rendering: There is a precise shrewdness that is itself unjust; and there is one who perverts a kindness to make a legal point; and there is a just man who humbles himself excessively.
translator_notes: Three types of distortion: cunning masquerading as wisdom, legalism corrupting generosity, and false humility.

verses.text_latin: Et est qui se submittit nimie a multa humilitate et est qui inclinat faciem suam et fingit se non videre quod ignoratum est.
verses.rendering: There is one who abases himself excessively out of great humility, and there is one who turns his face away and pretends not to see what is unrecognized.

verses.text_latin: Et si a viribus prohibeatur peccare si invenerit tempus malefaciet.
verses.rendering: And if he is prevented from sinning by lack of power, when he finds the opportunity, he will do evil.
translator_notes: A piercing observation: some people are virtuous only because they lack the means to sin. True character is revealed by opportunity.

verses.text_latin: Ex visu cognoscitur vir et ab occursu faciei cognoscitur sensatus.
verses.rendering: A person is known by his appearance, and a sensible man is recognized when you meet him face to face.
translator_notes: Reflects the ancient assumption that inner character is visible in outward bearing -- a physiognomic principle.

verses.text_latin: Amictus corporis et risus dentium et ingressus hominis enuntiant de illo.
verses.rendering: A person's clothing and his smile and his manner of walking declare what he is.

verses.text_latin: Est correptio mendax in ira contumeliosi et est iudicium quod non probatur esse bonum et est tacens et ipse est prudens.
verses.rendering: There is a rebuke that is a lie, spoken in the anger of an insolent man; and there is a judgment that is not proved to be just; and there is the silent one -- he is the prudent one.
translator_notes: The final maxim returns to the chapter's core theme: the wise person knows when to be silent.
